name: Kawaii fashion

lead: Kawaii fashion is the dressing side of kawaii ("cute") culture from Japan. It uses pastel colours, ribbons, frills, layered accessories and character motifs to create a soft, youthful, endearing look, in styles ranging from sweet Lolita and decora to fairy kei.

People use it to change how they present themselves, to look younger and sweeter, or to express identity. Its history runs through girls' magazines, 1970s handwriting trends, Sanrio's Hello Kitty and 1980s idols, and it has spread across Asia and the world.

paras: Wearers assemble outfits from the style's signature elements, such as pastel palettes, bows, lace, hair accessories, platform shoes and character goods, often following street-fashion magazines or Harajuku shops. Subtypes have their own rules.

There are no health risks to the clothing. Scholars have debated whether women are pressured to be cute, and some styles with childlike presentation attract critique; wearers describe the style as personal expression.

chain: Choose pastel colours, bows, lace and accessories
angle.text: Kawaii outfits change a person's look directly through colour, layering and accessories, producing a youthful, sweet appearance. Hair accessories and makeup in matching tones complete the look.

lead: Kawaii fashion is a family of Japanese-origin styles built on the concept of kawaii, meaning cute or adorable. It uses soft, youthful presentation, with pastel colours, bows, lace and layered accessories, to produce a sweet look.[1]

Kawaii as an aesthetic developed through shojo magazines, the illustrations of Rune Naito in the mid-20th century, 1970s teenage "cute handwriting", Sanrio's Hello Kitty in 1974 and 1980s idols such as Seiko Matsuda.[1] Major styles include Lolita (Victorian and Rococo-inspired, with sweet and gothic subtypes), decora (heavy accessory layering) and fairy kei (pastel, 1980s toy-inspired).[1]
By 2014 the Collins English Dictionary had added the word, and kawaii goods sell widely across East Asia and beyond.[1] Scholars have also discussed expectations placed on women to be cute.[1]

paras: The word kawaii evolved from an older term meaning "face aglow" and is traced by commentators to Sei Shonagon's Pillow Book. Girls' schools after 1899 and shojo media fostered girls' culture; illustrator Rune Naito drew baby-faced girls in the 1950s-70s and is credited with pioneering the aesthetic.[1]

Lolita draws on Victorian and Rococo dress with a "porcelain doll" goal; decora layers hairpins, bracelets and rings; fairy kei uses 1980s toy pastels, with the name reportedly from the magazine Zipper. Kimo-kawaii (creepy-cute) emerged in the 1990s and yami-kawaii (sickly-cute) in the mid-2010s.[1]

Hello Kitty sells in over 30 countries, and designer Sebastian Masuda of 6%DOKIDOKI has brought Harajuku street style to Western markets. Scholars argue women are socialised to be kawaii, and the term burikko describes women feigning childlike behaviour.[1]

timeline.event: Idols such as Seiko Matsuda popularise the cute look.[1]
